body.x: A conventional industrial gripper opens and closes, which works well for standardized, repetitive tasks. When the size, shape or position of objects keeps changing, factories often have to bring in dedicated tools or fixtures for each process or target object. Humanoid robots face a harder version of the same problem: to work in human environments they have to turn an object over after grasping it, insert it, assemble it and use tools.

Tesollo Inc., a robotics company in Yeonsu-gu, Incheon, that specializes in robot end effectors, builds multi-jointed grippers and five-finger robotic hands for that purpose. Founded in 2019 and led by CEO Youngjin Kim, the company will take part in FIX 2026 and was named a winner in the FIX 2026 Innovation Awards. Its stated aim at the show is to demonstrate the role multi-jointed robotic hands can play as the robotics industry moves beyond repetitive automation toward more complex tasks in real-world environments.

Tesollo says it has focused on the "hand," the final point of interaction between a robot and the physical world. It develops multi-degree-of-freedom (DoF) robotic hands whose joints can be controlled independently, so that one hand can grasp objects of various shapes and then perform tasks such as object reorientation, insertion, assembly and tool use. The company develops actuator modules, drive electronics, firmware, communication systems and control software for its hands, and provides software development kits (SDKs) and application programming interfaces (APIs) for integration with robot arms, vision systems and AI controllers. It says it has also moved into software, including AI-based grasp point generation and manipulation control, and that it does not tie its hands to a specific tactile sensor or robot platform.

The main product family is the Delto Gripper Series, with configurations of one to five fingers. At FIX 2026, Tesollo will present the DG-5F Series, a five-finger hand with 20 actively controlled degrees of freedom. The company says the DG-5F-M is designed for manipulation and research settings that need relatively high actuation capability, while the DG-5F-S keeps the 20-DoF architecture in a compact form weighing less than 1 kg, suited to integration with humanoid platforms. For industrial automation, it will also show the DG-3F-M, a 12-DoF three-finger gripper in which each finger has four independently controllable joints, which Tesollo says lets a single gripper handle objects of different sizes and shapes that would otherwise need different end effectors or fixtures.

At the exhibition, the company plans to show where conventional open-and-close grippers and multi-jointed hands are each most suitable, and how high-DoF hands apply in high-mix manufacturing and humanoid robotics, where objects and task requirements keep changing. It also wants to discuss practical applications with domestic and international robot manufacturers, manufacturing companies, system integrators, AI companies and robotics research institutions, since real-world manipulation requires robot arms, vision systems, AI and tactile sensors to work together.

Tesollo reports that its grippers and hands have been supplied to manufacturing companies, system integrators, universities and research institutions in Korea and to overseas markets including the U.S., China, Japan and Taiwan, reaching customers in about 20 countries. Research platforms at Stanford University, ETH Zurich and KAIST use its hands, the company says. It says Stanford's HandelBot and DexDrummer projects, presented publicly in 2026, used the 20-DoF DG-5F-M for research including two-handed cooperation, musical instrument performance and in-hand manipulation involving external contact. Overseas, the company says demand and inquiries are rising in the U.S. as robot learning and humanoid research expand, and that its products are used in manufacturing automation and research in Japan, China and Taiwan. It adds that it provides technical documentation, SDKs and APIs and is building local support through regional distributors and technology partners.

In industrial automation, Tesollo says it introduced a flexible automation solution with Techman Robot in 2026 that combines multi-jointed grippers with bin-picking for high-mix, low-volume manufacturing. It also signed an agreement with Megazone to cooperate on Physical AI education and technology using robotic hands and AI grippers. The company lists several milestones: the DG-5F was selected as one of Korea's Top 10 Mechanical Technologies of 2025, a product from the DG-3F series received recognition in the Robotics category of the CES 2025 Innovation Awards, and it was selected for Samsung Electronics' C-Lab Outside startup program in 2025. In 2026, it says it launched the DG-5F-S for global markets, completed a Series B funding round and expanded its production facilities, and it describes itself as moving beyond an R&D-focused stage toward higher production and overseas supply.

For overseas expansion, Tesollo plans to focus on North America, particularly the U.S., and on Japan and Germany. It names humanoid robot OEMs, manufacturing automation system integrators, and companies and research institutions working on robot learning and Physical AI as its primary potential partners. It says North America matters because of its investment in robot learning, embodied AI and humanoid robotics, and because multi-DoF hands can generate diverse manipulation data. It says Japan and Germany are looking for more flexible automation in response to labor shortages and the growth of high-mix production. Over the long term, the company says, the goal is to work with robot manufacturers, system integrators, sensor companies and AI companies in each region so its hands can serve as end-effector platforms across many kinds of robots.

The company's main difficulty is that a robotic hand business does not end with delivering hardware. The hand often has to be integrated with the customer's robot arm, control system, vision system, sensors and AI software, and customers use different robot platforms and communication protocols, which often calls for technical review and a proof of concept (PoC) before deployment. Tesollo says it continues to improve SDK and API documentation, sample code and Robot Operating System (ROS) integration materials. It also says it is hard to give overseas customers enough chances to test the hand directly, since specifications and demonstration videos do not fully convey performance, and that it is impractical to run demonstration equipment and engineers in every country. It therefore relies on local distributors, system integrators and robot manufacturers for demonstrations, support and maintenance, and plans to strengthen partner training, standardized technical documentation, remote support and local service alongside product reliability and production capacity.

Its plan is to expand applications across industrial automation, humanoid robotics and Physical AI. On hardware, it will keep advancing grippers and hands of different sizes and actuation capabilities with a focus on manufacturability, reliability, durability and maintainability. On software, it is working on AI-based grasp point generation and manipulation control to turn its hands from standalone hardware into integrated hardware and software platforms. In industrial automation, it plans to analyze the customer's process and validate the required grasping and manipulation before working with system integration partners to deploy on production lines, extending to insertion, assembly and fastening. For humanoids, it will keep improving the mechanical and electrical interfaces and SDKs and APIs so robot makers do not have to develop a whole hand themselves. The company says it does not aim to build a complete robot platform and wants to grow as a specialized provider of robotic hands that can be integrated into many robotic platforms.

Now in its third year, FIX 2026 (Future Innovation Technology Expo) is a future-industry exhibition that connects innovative technologies in future mobility, robotics, AI and ICT, and startups. It runs from Wednesday, Oct. 21, to Saturday, Oct. 24, at EXCO in Daegu. Under the theme "AI, Beyond Tech into Reality," the exhibition shares industry trends and core technologies through AI-based technology exhibitions, conferences and lectures by experts from Korea and abroad, and networking programs.
